# Perception on the Edge

::: {.callout-question}

How good does edge perception have to be, when every gain in accuracy costs
latency and energy?

:::

The robot has to notice the child walk in. A large detector spots her every
time, in any light, but runs at two frames a second and warms the board. A tiny
detector runs at thirty frames a second on almost no power, and loses her the
moment she steps out of the lamplight. Same task, same camera, two perception
systems that fail in opposite ways.

Which one ships? Neither, until you know what binds. The answer is a number, not
a preference.

## Accuracy is not free

On the edge, accuracy has a price, and it is paid in latency and energy. A bigger
model sees better. It also runs longer and draws more power, the two budgets a
body has least of. The reflex loop from [the loop chapter](00-from-tinyml-to-physical-ai.qmd)
sets a hard deadline, and a slower model misses it. The battery sets a hard
ceiling, and a hungrier model drains it.

::: {.column-margin}
**Properties in tension**: timeliness and energy, traded against accuracy. On the
edge, the first two usually bind first.
:::

So the question is never how accurate the model can be. It is how accurate it can
be inside the latency and energy budgets. And those budgets, as
[the elements](the-elements.qmd) showed, are usually where the binding constraint
sits.

## The cost before the model

Some of that cost is spent before the model runs at all. Raw signal has a size,
and moving it is not free. For a camera the rate is simple:

$$\text{data rate} = \text{pixels per frame} \times \text{framerate} \times \text{bytes per pixel}$$

A 640 by 480 feed at 30 frames a second, three bytes a pixel, is about 28
megabytes a second off the sensor before a single layer of the network has
touched it. Double the width and height for a sharper read and you quadruple the pixels, and
the rate.
Across the bus, into memory, and in the energy it takes to move each byte, that
raw rate often binds before the model's compute does. Predict it first. The
cheapest way to make perception fit is sometimes to sense less, not to shrink the
model.

## The knee

Accuracy against cost is not a straight line. @fig-knee draws its shape. While the
model is small, each bit of extra compute buys a lot of accuracy and the curve
climbs steeply. Past a point it flattens, and more compute buys almost nothing.
That bend is the knee, and it is the operating point worth choosing. Sit past it
and you spend latency and energy on accuracy you cannot use. Sit well before it
and you leave accuracy on the table that was nearly free.

::: {#fig-knee fig-cap="**The tradeoff knee**: accuracy rises steeply with cost, then flattens; the operating point worth choosing is the knee, not the peak." fig-alt="A curve of accuracy against cost that rises steeply, then levels off, with the knee marked as the operating point and the flat region beyond it labeled diminishing returns."}
![](../assets/diagrams/tradeoff-knee.svg)
:::

The knee is where you would sit if you could. The binding constraint decides
whether you can. If the latency or energy budget caps you to the left of the
knee, you live below it and accept the accuracy that fits. If the budget reaches
past the knee, you stop at the knee and bank the headroom. Either way the
operating point is a defended choice, named against a budget, not a model picked
because it was the newest.

Quantization is how you move along the curve cheaply. Dropping a model from
32-bit floats to 8-bit integers cuts its memory and speeds its arithmetic, often
by three to four times, for a small accuracy loss. It is the most common single
step from "too slow" to "fits." The lab measures what it actually costs you,
rather than trusting the rule of thumb.

## Build

::: {.callout-build title="Find your knee"}

Take one detector and run it at three operating points: a big model in the cloud,
a medium one on a laptop, and a small or quantized one on the device. Feed all
three the same inputs. At each point, measure three numbers: accuracy on your own
test clips, inferences per second, and milliwatts.

Plot accuracy against latency, and against energy. The knee will show itself.
Mark where your loop's deadline and your power budget fall, and pick the operating
point that sits at the knee, or at the budget, whichever comes first. Write one
sentence defending the choice by the budget that bound it.

If you cannot instrument power on your board, use the figures provided and reason
from them. The decision is the lesson, not the wattmeter.

:::

## What the number says

The quantized model rarely loses exactly the accuracy the datasheet implies, and
sometimes loses more, because your inputs are not the benchmark's. The cloud
model is the most accurate and almost never the right placement: its round trip
blows the loop deadline, just as [the loop chapter](00-from-tinyml-to-physical-ai.qmd)
predicted, and it ships the room's images off the device, which the privacy
budget may forbid outright. The three-point sweep is not there to crown the best
model. It is there to show you the curve, find its knee, and place perception
where the binding budget says it belongs.

## Read

The efficient-model literature is the toolbox for moving along this curve:
MobileNets (Howard et al., 2017) for architectures built to be cheap, and integer
quantization (Jacob et al., 2018) for running them in 8 bits with little loss.
MLPerf Tiny (Banbury et al., 2021) is the benchmark that reports accuracy,
latency, and energy together, which is the exact shape of the decision this
chapter asks you to make.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: run the same model at three operating points (cloud GPU, laptop, MCU)
  and have students watch accuracy, latency, and energy trade against one another
  before any theory. The curve convinces faster than the claim.
- **Open question**: how much TinyML do we assume versus reteach? This is the
  bridge chapter; students arrive on familiar ground, which buys goodwill before
  the harder closed-loop material.
- **Watch**: keep the chapter on the knee, not on quantization mechanics.
  Quantization is one way to move along the curve, not the subject.

:::
